_note: Cambridge B2 First — Reading and Use of English, Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze), 15 gaps. Extended practice beyond the exam's 8 gaps: each test is an original narrative with a funny twist at the end, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (two texts use only pool sets; the third adds two new INTUITY sets). Paragraphs in `text` carry NUMBERED {n} placeholders matched to the question whose `number` is n, so a renderer never counts gaps and one cannot drift onto the wrong question. Each question carries `focus`, `why` and a note per distractor, so a student learns the pattern, not just the answer.
title: Reading and Use of English — Part 1
timing: The whole paper is 1 hour 15 minutes. In the exam Part 1 has 8 gaps worth 8 marks of 52; these 15-gap texts are extended practice.
rubric: For questions 1–15, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap. There is an example at the beginning (0).

tests.title: Best-kept village
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (7.7 8.5 7.1 7.4 8.3 7.6 6.20 8.6 8.20 6.12 6.13 6.2 8.16 5.16 8.11)
text: In the summer of 1963, Little Barnford finished second in the county's Best-Kept Village competition for the eleventh year in a {0}. This year, the vicar announced, things would be different. The judging was due to {1} place on the first Saturday in August, and every household would be given a task. Farmer Gibbs was to trim the hedges around his {2}, the Women's Institute would repaint the bus shelter, and Mrs Pringle, who had once been to Paris, was put in charge of 'atmosphere'.

Nothing was left to chance. The vicar drew up the exact {3} the judge's car would take, timed to the minute. It would {4} him past the duck pond, the gleaming bus shelter and the church, which was {5} situated next to the tea tent. Children were reminded that they were not {6} to climb the war memorial, and a sign on the green asked visitors to {7} that the flower beds had just been planted. Mrs Pringle even {8} the vicarage cat with her own hairbrush, a hundred strokes every evening.

On the day, record {9} of visitors crowded onto the green. The judge, a retired colonel, arrived at ten, and the vicar {10} him to everyone who mattered. We were extremely {11} to have perfect weather, and the sixpenny entrance fee {12} tea, scones and a concert by the school choir. Mrs Pringle asked me to {13} the cake stall for a moment. Everything was going beautifully.

Then, at exactly twelve o'clock, Farmer Gibbs's bird-scarer {14} with a bang like a cannon. The colonel, who had spent the war dodging real ones, threw himself flat into the duck pond. He climbed out dripping, with a lily pad on his head, and nobody could explain how such a thing could {15}. A week later the results arrived. Little Barnford had come second again, but the colonel had invented a special award just for us: 'Most Exciting Village in the County'. By the following spring, every village in the county had bought a bird-scarer.

example.why: 'In a row' is the fixed phrase for things that happen one after another. 'Line', 'series' and 'chain' do not complete the phrase.

questions.why: An event takes place; 'take place' is the fixed phrase for something being held.

distractors.hold: you hold an event, but you cannot 'hold place'

questions.why: Hedges surround a farmer's fields, the land where he grows crops or keeps animals.

distractors.areas: is too general and does not describe a farmer's land
distractors.places: is too general; hedges do not go round 'places'

questions.why: The road a vehicle follows from start to finish is its route; 'the route the car would take'.

distractors.path: is a narrow track for walking, not for a car
distractors.way: does not go with 'drew up' and 'timed to the minute'
distractors.lane: is a narrow country road or part of a motorway, not a planned journey

questions.why: A route leads you somewhere: it takes you past or to places.

distractors.head: 'head' in this sense has no object; you head somewhere yourself
distractors.proceed: cannot take an object: you proceed, you do not proceed someone

questions.why: 'Conveniently situated' means in a useful, easy-to-reach position.

distractors.efficiently: describes how work is done, not where a building is

questions.why: 'Not be supposed to' means not be allowed to.

distractors.wondered: cannot be followed by 'to + infinitive' in the passive
distractors.judged: 'judged to' means considered to be, not allowed
distractors.doubted: does not take 'to + infinitive' in this way

questions.why: 'Please note that' is the standard way a notice asks people to pay attention to a fact.

distractors.discover: means find out something unknown, not read a notice
distractors.find: 'find that' means learn from experience, not pay attention

questions.why: With a hairbrush you brush hair or fur.

distractors.cleaned: means removing dirt, not what a hairbrush does
distractors.swept: is what you do to a floor with a broom
distractors.polished: is for shoes, silver or furniture, not a cat

questions.why: 'Record numbers of' is used with countable nouns such as visitors.

distractors.amounts: is for uncountable nouns like money or time
distractors.quantities: is for things and substances, not people

questions.why: You introduce someone to someone else, so 'introduced him to everyone'.

distractors.begun: is a past participle and cannot follow 'the vicar' alone
distractors.taught: 'taught him to' needs a verb, not a person
distractors.explained: you explain something to someone, not a person to people

questions.why: 'Fortunate to have' means lucky to have.

distractors.reasonable: means fair or sensible, not lucky
distractors.appropriate: means right for the situation and does not describe luck
distractors.suitable: means right for a purpose, not lucky

questions.why: A price or fee includes the things you get for it.

distractors.consisted: needs 'of' and describes what something is made of
distractors.featured: is used for shows or products, not what a fee covers
distractors.composed: needs 'of' in the passive: be composed of

questions.why: To watch a stall is to keep an eye on it for someone.

distractors.allow: needs a person and an action: allow someone to do
distractors.look: needs a preposition: look after the stall
distractors.permit: means allow and needs a person and an action

questions.why: An alarm, bomb or bird-scarer goes off when it suddenly makes a loud noise.

distractors.burst out: is used for people suddenly laughing or crying
distractors.broke out: is used for fires, wars and diseases starting
distractors.set off: without an object means to start a journey

questions.why: Things happen; 'how such a thing could happen' is the natural phrase.

distractors.go: 'how it could go' asks how it went, not why it occurred
distractors.come: 'come' needs a continuation such as 'come about'
distractors.arrive: is used for people and things reaching a place

tests.title: The Riviera Parasol
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (6.10 5.19 7.19 5.17 8.15 6.15 7.13 7.14 6.6 7.3 7.9 5.20 7.10 8.9 8.19)
text: Higginbottom's of Wetherby had been making umbrellas for well {0} a century, and was known {1} the finest umbrella maker in the north of England. But in the long, dry summer of 1964, sales had {2} for the fourth month in a row, and the company was fast {3} out of cash. The problem was {4} due to the weather, although young Leonard Higginbottom's habit of giving umbrellas away to customers who had forgotten their own had not helped. 'You {5} not to have given away three hundred of them,' his father told him sternly.

The bank refused to lend them the enormous {6} of money they needed, and at an emergency meeting old Mr Higginbottom {7} it perfectly clear that he would rather close the factory than sell it. 'It makes no {8} to sell umbrellas to people who have forgotten what rain looks like,' sighed the accountant. 'And price is only one {9} of the problem.'

It was Mrs Higginbottom, who did the books on Fridays, who asked them to look at the other {10} of the coin. Nobody wanted umbrellas, she pointed out, but everybody wanted shade. 'So Mrs Higginbottom {11} that we paint them white and sell them as sunshades,' said the accountant slowly. The factory {12} all its efforts on the new 'Riviera Parasol', and the engineers soon {13} how to make the handles long enough to push into the sand. Leonard was put in charge of {14} advertisements in every seaside newspaper from Scarborough to Brighton.

The Riviera Parasol reached the shops on the first of August. That very morning, it began to rain, and it did not stop for six weeks. Leonard did not {15} in selling a single parasol to a sunbather, but by September every one had gone, bought by soaked holidaymakers who had left their umbrellas at home. Ever since, Higginbottom's has painted every umbrella white. So far, it has rained every summer.

example.why: 'Well over' a number or period means a lot more than it. 'Above', 'beyond' and 'upon' do not combine with 'well' before a length of time.

questions.why: 'Known as' gives the name or description people use for someone or something.

distractors.by: 'known by' means recognised by someone, not described as
distractors.about: 'known about' means people have information about it

questions.why: Sales, prices and figures fall when they go down.

distractors.descended: is used for going down stairs or hills, not sales
distractors.shortened: is used for length or time, not figures
distractors.subtracted: is a maths verb and needs an object

questions.why: 'Run out of' means have none left; 'fast running out of cash'.

distractors.dropping: 'drop out of' means leave a course or race
distractors.growing: 'grow out of' means become too big for something
distractors.falling: 'fall out of' means drop from something, or stop being friends

questions.why: 'Largely due to' means mainly because of.

distractors.badly: means poorly or seriously, and does not go with 'due to'
distractors.extremely: intensifies adjectives such as 'hot', not 'due to'
distractors.highly: goes with words like 'likely' or 'successful', not 'due to'

questions.why: 'Ought not to have done' criticises a past action; only 'ought' is followed by 'to'.

distractors.need: the past criticism is 'need not have', without 'to'

questions.why: 'A sum of money' is the fixed phrase for an amount of money.

distractors.number: is for countable things, not money
distractors.total: is not followed by 'of money' in this way
distractors.figure: is a number on paper, not 'a figure of money'

questions.why: 'Make it clear that' means state something firmly so no one can misunderstand.

distractors.done: is a past participle and does not form the phrase

questions.why: 'It makes no sense to' means it is not logical to.

distractors.case: you make a case for something, not 'no case to'
distractors.reason: you have a reason, you do not 'make no reason'

questions.why: An aspect is one part or feature of a problem or situation.

distractors.appearance: means how something looks or the act of appearing

questions.why: 'The other side of the coin' means the opposite way of looking at a situation.

distractors.half: a coin has two sides, not two halves

questions.why: You propose that someone does something; it takes a that-clause about a plan.

distractors.provides: means supplies and does not take 'that we paint'
distractors.offers: is followed by 'to do' or an object, not a that-clause
distractors.contributes: needs 'to' and means give a share

questions.why: You concentrate your efforts on something when you give it all your attention.

distractors.thought: you think about something; you do not think efforts
distractors.engaged: 'engaged in' describes taking part, not focusing efforts
distractors.occupied: 'occupied with' describes being busy, not directing effort

questions.why: 'Work out how to' means find the solution to a problem by thinking.

distractors.drawn up: is a participle, and 'draw up' is used for plans and documents
distractors.carried out: is a participle, and 'carry out' means perform a task
distractors.set up: means start a business or arrange equipment, not solve a problem

questions.why: You place an advertisement in a newspaper when you pay for it to appear there.

distractors.producing: means creating it, which does not fit 'in every newspaper'
distractors.forming: is used for groups or shapes, not advertisements
distractors.making: means designing it, not arranging for it to appear

questions.why: 'Succeed in + -ing' means manage to do something.

distractors.deal: 'deal in' means trade in goods, and does not mean manage

tests.title: The great novel
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (5.14 7.11 6.18 8.14 8.17 5.18 7.20 6.7 6.9 6.4 7.8 8.18 8.2) and two new INTUITY sets
text: My Uncle Albert {0} up his mind to write a bestseller on a wet Tuesday in 1966. He was not only the village postman but {1} the secretary of the chess club, so he felt he knew a great deal about both adventure and suspense. The book would be loosely {2} on his own life, which was unfortunate, because nothing had ever happened in it.

He signed up for an evening class at the library, where the tutor, Miss Fenwick, was so {3} that she praised even his spelling. '{4} every sentence carefully before you put it on paper,' she advised, and Albert did, very slowly. Aunt Doris kept him {5} with enough tea and biscuits to survive a siege, and told the neighbours, 'He {6} out to the garden shed at seven every evening, and we don't see him again until midnight.'

The trouble was Mr Platt next door, who had just taken up the trumpet. Night after night, his scales began to {7} Albert to distraction. Albert kept writing, {8} though he could hardly hear himself think, and by Christmas he was so exhausted {9} he fell asleep over his typewriter most nights. Worse still, his thrilling spy story had somehow {10} a fairy tale about a frog. 'Could you {11} a good publisher?' he asked Miss Fenwick. She gave him six names. The manuscript was rejected {12} every one of them.

In the spring Albert {13} an advertisement in the local paper for a short-story competition, with a first {14} of fifty pounds. He entered the frog. He did not win. The winner was Mr Platt, with a hilarious tale about a man next door who typed all night and kept the whole street awake. Albert {15} he had never touched a typewriter. Mr Platt spent the money on a new trumpet.

example.why: 'Make up your mind' is the fixed phrase for deciding. 'Take', 'set' and 'put' do not form a phrase with 'up his mind'.

questions.why: 'Not only ... but also' is a fixed pair that adds a second, surprising fact.

distractors.in addition: cannot follow 'but' in this structure; it needs 'to' or a new sentence
distractors.together: means with other people, not as well
distractors.as well as: cannot follow 'but' and needs a noun or -ing after it

questions.why: A book is based on real events or a person's life.

distractors.located: is for places: located in a town
distractors.settled: means living permanently somewhere, or decided
distractors.formed: means made or created, and does not go with 'on'

questions.why: An encouraging teacher praises and gives confidence, which is why she praised his spelling.

distractors.productive: means producing a lot of work, not praising others
distractors.dependable: means reliable, which does not explain the praise
distractors.creative: means imaginative, which does not explain the praise

questions.why: 'Consider' means think carefully about, which matches 'carefully before you put it on paper'.

distractors.Suppose: introduces an imagined situation with a clause, not an object
distractors.Imagine: means picture in your mind, not check carefully

questions.why: 'Keep someone supplied with' means make sure they always have enough of something.

distractors.stored: is used for things kept away, not people
distractors.carried: does not take 'with' for food you receive

questions.why: 'Slip out' means leave quietly without being noticed.

distractors.chops: means cutting with a heavy blade
distractors.cuts: 'cut out' means remove or stop doing something
distractors.dips: means put something briefly into a liquid

questions.why: 'Drive someone to distraction' means annoy them until they cannot think.

distractors.continue: cannot take a person and 'to distraction'
distractors.go: cannot take a person as its object here
distractors.let: 'let' needs a verb after the person, not 'to distraction'

questions.why: 'Even though' introduces a strong contrast: he continued despite the noise.

distractors.however: is not followed by 'though' and needs a new clause
distractors.whereas: compares two facts and cannot be followed by 'though'

questions.why: 'So + adjective + that' shows a result: he was so tired that he fell asleep.

distractors.while: means during the time that, which breaks the structure

questions.why: 'Turn into' means change and become something else.

distractors.brought off: means succeed in doing something difficult
distractors.caught on: means become popular and has no object
distractors.taken over: means take control of a company or place

questions.why: To recommend something is to suggest it as good.

distractors.approve: means agree officially, and needs 'of' for opinions
distractors.notice: means see or become aware of

questions.why: In the passive, the person who does the action follows 'by'.

distractors.as: would describe a role, not who did the rejecting
distractors.for: would mean on behalf of, not who rejected it

questions.why: 'Come across' means find something by chance.

distractors.found out: is for learning a fact, not finding an object

questions.why: Competitions offer a first prize.

distractors.reward: is given for help or good behaviour, not for winning a competition
distractors.award: does not form the phrase 'first award' for a competition

questions.why: 'Wish + past perfect' expresses regret about the past.

distractors.requested: means asked for formally and cannot express regret
